excerpt:
**Q: Why can't we use Mean Squared Error (MSE) for Logistic Regression?**
A: Logistic Regression passes the linear combination $z$ through a Sigmoid activation function. If you insert a Sigmoid function inside the MSE equation, the resulting mathematical landscape becomes non-convex. It will have multiple local minima, meaning Gradient Descent is highly likely to get stuck and fail to find the optimal solution. We use Log Loss (Binary Cross-Entropy) because it guarantees a convex landscape.
source_id: ai-course:09 - Quizzes and Question Banks/03. Question Series/Qs1.md
source_path: 09 - Quizzes and Question Banks/03. Question Series/Qs1.md

excerpt:
**Q: What is the purpose of the bias term ($b$)?**
A: While weights ($w$) determine the slope or importance of an input, the bias ($b$) shifts the activation function left or right. Without a bias, the activation function must always cross the origin $(0,0)$, which severely limits the patterns the network can learn.

excerpt:
> [!info] Note Overview
> This note covers the foundational concepts of **Residuals**, **Residual Mapping**, and **Residual Learning**, which form the backbone of the ResNet (Residual Network) architecture. This concept is arguably one of the most important innovations in modern deep learning, heavily utilized not just in Computer Vision (CNNs), but also in modern NLP models like Transformers.
source_id: ai-course:09 - Quizzes and Question Banks/03. Question Series/Qs3.md
source_path: 09 - Quizzes and Question Banks/03. Question Series/Qs3.md

excerpt: Before diving into residuals, it is critical to understand *why* this concept was invented. You must remember two major roadblocks that occur when training very deep neural networks (e.g., networks with 50, 100, or 1000 layers).
source_id: ai-course:09 - Quizzes and Question Banks/03. Question Series/Qs3.md
source_path: 09 - Quizzes and Question Banks/03. Question Series/Qs3.md

excerpt: In standard feed-forward networks, gradients are calculated using the Chain Rule during backpropagation. As errors propagate backward from the output to the input layers, they are repeatedly multiplied by weight matrices and derivatives of activation functions. If these numbers are small (less than 1), the gradients shrink exponentially until they "vanish" to zero. **Result:** The early layers stop learning.
source_id: ai-course:09 - Quizzes and Question Banks/03. Question Series/Qs3.md
source_path: 09 - Quizzes and Question Banks/03. Question Series/Qs3.md

excerpt: Even if we fix vanishing gradients using techniques like Batch Normalization and proper weight initialization, deep networks suffer from the **Degradation Problem**.
source_id: ai-course:09 - Quizzes and Question Banks/03. Question Series/Qs3.md
source_path: 09 - Quizzes and Question Banks/03. Question Series/Qs3.md

excerpt:
* **The Theory:** A deep network should perform *at least as well* as a shallow one. If you take a 20-layer network and add 30 layers to it, the model could theoretically just learn the "Identity Function" (passing the input exactly as it is) for those 30 extra layers.
* **The Reality:** Empirically, as network depth increases, accuracy gets saturated and then rapidly degrades. **This is not caused by overfitting** (training error actually *increases* alongside test error). It happens because modern optimization algorithms (like SGD or Adam) struggle incredibly hard to learn the identity function from a complex stack of non-linear layers.
source_id: ai-course:09 - Quizzes and Question Banks/03. Question Series/Qs3.md
source_path: 09 - Quizzes and Question Banks/03. Question Series/Qs3.md

excerpt:
> [!tip] What students often miss
> Students frequently confuse the Degradation Problem with Overfitting. Remember: **Overfitting** means training error is low and test error is high. **Degradation** means both training and test errors are high. The network simply becomes mathematically harder to optimize.
source_id: ai-course:09 - Quizzes and Question Banks/03. Question Series/Qs3.md
source_path: 09 - Quizzes and Question Banks/03. Question Series/Qs3.md

excerpt: To solve the degradation problem, researchers redefined what the network actually learns. But first, what is a residual?
source_id: ai-course:09 - Quizzes and Question Banks/03. Question Series/Qs3.md
source_path: 09 - Quizzes and Question Banks/03. Question Series/Qs3.md

excerpt: Traditionally, a **residual** is defined as the difference between an observed (true) value and an estimated (predicted) value. It is the "error" or the "leftover" part that your model failed to capture.
source_id: ai-course:09 - Quizzes and Question Banks/03. Question Series/Qs3.md
source_path: 09 - Quizzes and Question Banks/03. Question Series/Qs3.md

excerpt: $$ \text{Residual} = \text{True Value} - \text{Predicted Value} $$
source_id: ai-course:09 - Quizzes and Question Banks/03. Question Series/Qs3.md
source_path: 09 - Quizzes and Question Banks/03. Question Series/Qs3.md

excerpt: *Example:* If the true house price is $10$, and your model predicts $8$, the residual is $2$.
source_id: ai-course:09 - Quizzes and Question Banks/03. Question Series/Qs3.md
source_path: 09 - Quizzes and Question Banks/03. Question Series/Qs3.md

excerpt: Deep learning borrows this conceptual framework but applies it structurally to the *transformations* inside the network. Instead of a residual being an "error," it represents the **difference between the input data and the desired underlying mapping**.
source_id: ai-course:09 - Quizzes and Question Banks/03. Question Series/Qs3.md
source_path: 09 - Quizzes and Question Banks/03. Question Series/Qs3.md

excerpt: To understand Residual Learning, we must define two different functions: the Underlying Mapping $H(x)$ and the Residual Mapping $F(x)$.
source_id: ai-course:09 - Quizzes and Question Banks/03. Question Series/Qs3.md
source_path: 09 - Quizzes and Question Banks/03. Question Series/Qs3.md

excerpt:
In a traditional neural network, you pass an input $x$ into a stack of layers. You want these layers to figure out a complex transformation, which we call $H(x)$. 
The network tries to learn this entire, heavy mapping directly from scratch.
heading_path: The Old Way: Learning the Underlying Mapping $H(x)$
source_id: ai-course:09 - Quizzes and Question Banks/03. Question Series/Qs3.md
source_path: 09 - Quizzes and Question Banks/03. Question Series/Qs3.md

excerpt: $$ \text{Network Output} = H(x) $$
heading_path: The Old Way: Learning the Underlying Mapping $H(x)$
source_id: ai-course:09 - Quizzes and Question Banks/03. Question Series/Qs3.md
source_path: 09 - Quizzes and Question Banks/03. Question Series/Qs3.md

excerpt: Researchers realized: *What if, instead of forcing the layers to learn the entire complex transformation $H(x)$, we just ask them to learn the DIFFERENCE between the input $x$ and the output $H(x)$?*
heading_path: The New Way: Learning the Residual Mapping $F(x)$
source_id: ai-course:09 - Quizzes and Question Banks/03. Question Series/Qs3.md
source_path: 09 - Quizzes and Question Banks/03. Question Series/Qs3.md

excerpt: We define this difference as the **Residual Mapping**, $F(x)$:
heading_path: The New Way: Learning the Residual Mapping $F(x)$
source_id: ai-course:09 - Quizzes and Question Banks/03. Question Series/Qs3.md
source_path: 09 - Quizzes and Question Banks/03. Question Series/Qs3.md

heading_path: The New Way: Learning the Residual Mapping $F(x)$
source_id: ai-course:09 - Quizzes and Question Banks/03. Question Series/Qs3.md
source_path: 09 - Quizzes and Question Banks/03. Question Series/Qs3.md

excerpt: Using basic algebra, we can rearrange this formula to see what the final output of our network block should be:
heading_path: The New Way: Learning the Residual Mapping $F(x)$
source_id: ai-course:09 - Quizzes and Question Banks/03. Question Series/Qs3.md
source_path: 09 - Quizzes and Question Banks/03. Question Series/Qs3.md

heading_path: The New Way: Learning the Residual Mapping $F(x)$
source_id: ai-course:09 - Quizzes and Question Banks/03. Question Series/Qs3.md
source_path: 09 - Quizzes and Question Banks/03. Question Series/Qs3.md

excerpt: Instead of mapping $x \rightarrow H(x)$, the network now maps $x \rightarrow F(x)$. The original input $x$ is simply added back to the learned residual $F(x)$ at the very end.
heading_path: The New Way: Learning the Residual Mapping $F(x)$
source_id: ai-course:09 - Quizzes and Question Banks/03. Question Series/Qs3.md
source_path: 09 - Quizzes and Question Banks/03. Question Series/Qs3.md

excerpt: **Residual Learning** is the training strategy where a neural network is explicitly designed to learn $F(x)$ rather than $H(x)$.
source_id: ai-course:09 - Quizzes and Question Banks/03. Question Series/Qs3.md
source_path: 09 - Quizzes and Question Banks/03. Question Series/Qs3.md

excerpt: To implement this mathematically in code, we use a structural mechanism called a **Skip Connection** (also known as a Shortcut Connection).
source_id: ai-course:09 - Quizzes and Question Banks/03. Question Series/Qs3.md
source_path: 09 - Quizzes and Question Banks/03. Question Series/Qs3.md

excerpt: A skip connection literally takes the input $x$, bypasses (skips) one or more convolutional layers, and adds it directly to the output of those layers.
source_id: ai-course:09 - Quizzes and Question Banks/03. Question Series/Qs3.md
source_path: 09 - Quizzes and Question Banks/03. Question Series/Qs3.md

excerpt:
```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A[Input: x] --> B[Weight Layer e.g., Conv2D]
    A -->|Skip Connection / Shortcut| E
    
    B --> C[Activation: ReLU]
    C --> D[Weight Layer e.g., Conv2D]
    
    D -->|Learned Residual: Fx| E((+ Addition Gate))
    
    E --> F[Activation: ReLU]
    F --> G[Output: Hx = Fx + x]

    classDef default fill:#1e1e1e,stroke:#4CAF50,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    classDef addition fill:#4CAF50,stroke:#fff,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    class E addition;
```
source_id: ai-course:09 - Quizzes and Question Banks/03. Question Series/Qs3.md
source_path: 09 - Quizzes and Question Banks/03. Question Series/Qs3.md

excerpt:
> [!warning] Critical Detail: Element-wise Addition
> The addition performed at the `+` gate is **element-wise**. This means the dimensions of $F(x)$ and $x$ MUST be perfectly identical. 
> *What happens if the dimensions change?* (e.g., the convolution layer reduces the spatial size or increases the channel count). 
> **Solution:** A $1 \times 1$ Convolution is applied to the skip connection path to strictly project the input $x$ into the correct shape before the addition occurs.
source_id: ai-course:09 - Quizzes and Question Banks/03. Question Series/Qs3.md
source_path: 09 - Quizzes and Question Banks/03. Question Series/Qs3.md

excerpt: Why did this simple addition $F(x) + x$ allow researchers to suddenly train 152-layer networks (ResNet-152) and win every Computer Vision competition?
heading_path: 5. Why Residual Learning Solves the Problems
source_id: ai-course:09 - Quizzes and Question Banks/03. Question Series/Qs3.md
source_path: 09 - Quizzes and Question Banks/03. Question Series/Qs3.md

excerpt: Remember the Degradation Problem? We wanted extra layers in deep networks to just learn the "Identity Function" if they weren't needed.
heading_path: 5. Why Residual Learning Solves the Problems
source_id: ai-course:09 - Quizzes and Question Banks/03. Question Series/Qs3.md
source_path: 09 - Quizzes and Question Banks/03. Question Series/Qs3.md

excerpt:
* **Without Residuals:** Learning $H(x) = x$ requires a complex matrix of weights to perfectly mirror the input. Neural networks are incredibly bad at doing this through non-linear activations like ReLU.
* **With Residuals:** The output is $H(x) = F(x) + x$. If the optimal transformation is just to pass the input forward (the identity mapping), the network only has to learn to push the weights of $F(x)$ to **$0$**.
heading_path: 5. Why Residual Learning Solves the Problems
source_id: ai-course:09 - Quizzes and Question Banks/03. Question Series/Qs3.md
source_path: 09 - Quizzes and Question Banks/03. Question Series/Qs3.md

excerpt: Learning $F(x) = 0$ is trivially easy for an optimizer because it just pushes weights toward zero using L2 Regularization (Weight Decay).
heading_path: 5. Why Residual Learning Solves the Problems
source_id: ai-course:09 - Quizzes and Question Banks/03. Question Series/Qs3.md
source_path: 09 - Quizzes and Question Banks/03. Question Series/Qs3.md

excerpt:
Skip connections act as an "express highway" for gradients during backpropagation. 
Let's look at the derivative of the output with respect to the input:
heading_path: 5. Why Residual Learning Solves the Problems
B. Smooth Gradient Flow (Fixing Vanishing Gradients)
source_id: ai-course:09 - Quizzes and Question Banks/03. Question Series/Qs3.md
source_path: 09 - Quizzes and Question Banks/03. Question Series/Qs3.md

excerpt: $$ \frac{\partial H}{\partial x} = \frac{\partial (F(x) + x)}{\partial x} = \frac{\partial F}{\partial x} + 1 $$
heading_path: 5. Why Residual Learning Solves the Problems
B. Smooth Gradient Flow (Fixing Vanishing Gradients)
source_id: ai-course:09 - Quizzes and Question Banks/03. Question Series/Qs3.md
source_path: 09 - Quizzes and Question Banks/03. Question Series/Qs3.md

excerpt: That **$+ 1$** is pure magic. Even if the gradients passing through the complex layers ($\frac{\partial F}{\partial x}$) become infinitely small (vanish), the $+ 1$ ensures that a gradient of at least $1$ is safely propagated backward to the earlier layers. Early layers *always* get a strong signal to learn from.
heading_path: 5. Why Residual Learning Solves the Problems
B. Smooth Gradient Flow (Fixing Vanishing Gradients)

source_id: ai-course:09 - Quizzes and Question Banks/03. Question Series/Qs3.md
source_path: 09 - Quizzes and Question Banks/03. Question Series/Qs3.md

excerpt: Imagine you are an artist who drew a sketch of a landscape ($x$). You hand it to a master painter (the neural network) to create a perfect, polished masterpiece ($H(x)$).
source_id: ai-course:09 - Quizzes and Question Banks/03. Question Series/Qs3.md
source_path: 09 - Quizzes and Question Banks/03. Question Series/Qs3.md

excerpt:
* **Option A (Traditional Deep Learning):** You give the painter a blank canvas. They must look at your sketch, throw it away, and try to perfectly redraw the landscape from scratch, while also making it a masterpiece. This takes immense effort, and they might mess up the underlying proportions.
* **Option B (Residual Learning):** You hand the sketch directly to the master painter on a semi-transparent canvas. The painter *only* needs to paint over the flaws, add shading, and make small corrections ($F(x)$). Their corrections are then combined with your original sketch ($F(x) + x$) to form the masterpiece.
source_id: ai-course:09 - Quizzes and Question Banks/03. Question Series/Qs3.md
source_path: 09 - Quizzes and Question Banks/03. Question Series/Qs3.md

excerpt: Residual learning is simply: **"Learn the corrections, do not relearn the foundation."**
source_id: ai-course:09 - Quizzes and Question Banks/03. Question Series/Qs3.md
source_path: 09 - Quizzes and Question Banks/03. Question Series/Qs3.md

excerpt: For quick recall and exam/interview preparation, memorize this table:
source_id: ai-course:09 - Quizzes and Question Banks/03. Question Series/Qs3.md
source_path: 09 - Quizzes and Question Banks/03. Question Series/Qs3.md

excerpt:
| Term | Definition / Role in Neural Networks | Formula |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Residual** | The difference between the desired mapping and the original input. | $H(x) - x$ |
| **Underlying Mapping** | The complete, final transformation we actually want to achieve. | $H(x)$ |
| **Residual Mapping** | The specific correction/adjustment the intermediate layers learn. | $F(x) = H(x) - x$ |
| **Skip Connection** | The structural architecture (the wire bypassing layers) that performs the addition operation. | N/A |
| **Final Output** | The combination of the learned correction and the bypassed original input. | $H(x) = F(x) + x$ |
source_id: ai-course:09 - Quizzes and Question Banks/03. Question Series/Qs3.md
source_path: 09 - Quizzes and Question Banks/03. Question Series/Qs3.md

excerpt:
> [!tip] Ultimate Takeaway
> Without skip connections, networks deeper than ~30 layers suffer severely from degradation. With skip connections, networks can easily exceed 100+ layers (ResNet-101, ResNet-152), enjoying stable gradients and highly efficient optimization. This single mathematical addition changed Deep Learning forever.
